my_sentence: Someone lending me some money bothers me the most.
correction: If someone asks me to lend him or her some money, that bothers me the most.
explanation: The natural structure is "ask someone to lend..." inside an "if" clause. The teacher modeled "If someone asks me to lend him or her some money."
correct_examples: If someone asks me to lend them money, I feel uneasy.
He asked me to lend him my car.
context: Discussing which favors bother him most.

my_sentence: They can't return and you will lose your friend.
correction: They don't return it, and then you'll lose your friendship.
explanation: What you lose is the "friendship" (the relationship), not "your friend"; and "return" needs the object "it." The teacher gave "you'll lose your friendship."
correct_examples: If they don't pay it back, you lose the friendship.
Money problems can end a friendship.
context: Why lending money to friends is risky.

my_sentence: If your relationship was terrible, it was too embarrassed to stay together.
correction: If your relationship is terrible, it is too embarrassing to stay together.
explanation: Use "-ing" adjectives for something that causes the feeling: a situation is "embarrassing." "Embarrassed" (-ed) describes the person who feels it. The teacher corrected "it is too embarrassing."
correct_examples: It is embarrassing to ask for money back.
context: Why losing a friendship over money is awkward.

my_sentence: It depends on the serious of the accident.
correction: It depends on the seriousness of the accident.
explanation: The noun form is "seriousness"; "serious" is the adjective. After "the ... of" you need the noun. The teacher repeated "seriousness."
correct_examples: It depends on the seriousness of the problem.
The cost depends on the seriousness of the damage.
context: How much to pay after a car accident.

my_sentence: If they want to go to the hospital, I can send them to there.
correction: If they want to go to the hospital, I can drive them there.
explanation: For taking a person somewhere by car, use "drive them there," not "send them"; and "there" takes no "to." The teacher corrected "I can drive them there, not send."
correct_examples: I can drive you there tomorrow.
She drove me to the station.
context: Offering an alternative to lending his car.

my_sentence: I have ever done this many times before.
correction: I have done that many times before.
explanation: In affirmative present-perfect statements, don't use "ever"; say "I have done that." "Ever" belongs in questions ("Have you ever...?"). The teacher gave "I have done that."
correct_examples: I have done that many times.
Have you ever done that before?
context: Saying he had helped friends move before.

my_sentence: When I started my job, I rent an apartment with different people.
correction: When I started my job, I rented an apartment with different people.
explanation: This is a completed past event, so use the past tense "rented," matching "started." The teacher supplied "rented."
correct_examples: I rented a small flat after graduation.
We rented a car for the trip last year.
context: Recalling his first apartment when he started working.

my_sentence: Our printers are very convenient and easily to use.
correction: Our printers are very convenient and easy to use.
explanation: Use the adjective "easy" before "to use," not the adverb "easily." The teacher corrected "easy, not easily, easy to use."
correct_examples: This app is easy to use.
The machine is simple and easy to operate.
context: Comparing modern printers with older machines.
